How to Build the LEGO Crane

Twelve steps, from the baseplate upward

These steps are a reconstruction, not a record. They were read off photographs of the finished bird, so the piece sizes are one plausible way to reach that shape rather than the exact pieces that were used. Two places are reasoned rather than seen, and say so where they come up: the rectangular bricks inside the body, which the wings hide, and the legs, which are hard to photograph in black. Substitute freely for whatever is in the bin — choosing the substitute is the design work, not a compromise.

Pieces you will need

1 green baseplate, 16 × 8
2 black 1 × 1 plates (feet)
2 black 1 × 1 columns
2 black 1 × 1 plates (tops)
1 white 2 × 9 brick
1 white 2 × 7 brick
2 white wedges
2 light gray 1 × 2 blades
2 white 2 × 2 blades
1 black 3 × 2 inverted slope
1 light gray 3 × 2 slope
1 white 2 × 2 brick
1 light gray 2 × 3 brick
1 light gray ridged plate
1 light gray 2 × 3 plate
1 white 2 × 2 slope
1 light gray 1 × 2 brick (seat)
1 light gray 1 × 1 × 4 column
1 black 2 × 2 brick
1 white 1 × 1 round tile
1 red 2 × 2 slope
1 black 2 × 3 plate
2 yellow inverted slopes
1 yellow cone
1

Start with the baseplate

One green baseplate, 16 × 8. Set it down with the long side facing you — the crane will face to the right, and will very nearly fill it.

Add these pieces
1 green baseplate, 16 × 8
2

Stand up the two legs

Three pieces each: a short one on the baseplate, a long one for the span, a short one on top. The long piece reaches and the short ones join, which is where the strength is. Least certain step in the sheet — black photographs badly, and this is read from a dark picture.

Add these pieces
2 black 1 × 1 plates (feet)
2 black 1 × 1 columns
2 black 1 × 1 plates (tops)
3

Lay the body's rectangular core

Two plain courses of rectangular brick. Almost none of this will show once the wings go on — it is the thing everything else mounts to. Inferred: the wings hide these bricks in every photograph, but a strip of the body's top edge is visible above the wing, so their size is read from the outline rather than guessed.

Add these pieces
1 white 2 × 9 brick
1 white 2 × 7 brick
4

Mount the wings on the core

Three pieces a side, flanking the core at the same height so they hide it. The back is a wedge — tilted on top and drawn in at the sides at once — and the two pieces in front of it thin toward the leading edge because their tops and undersides both slope away. Three pieces carry nearly all of the bird's curve.

Add these pieces
2 white wedges
2 light gray 1 × 2 blades
2 white 2 × 2 blades
5

Taper the tail

Two slopes make the tail a POINT: the gray one on top falls away toward the back, and the black one beneath is inverted, so its underside rises to meet it. Between them the body closes to a thin edge instead of a chopped corner, and the gray face becomes the long straight line of the bird's back. The black is expedience — it is what the bin had.

Add these pieces
1 black 3 × 2 inverted slope
1 light gray 3 × 2 slope
6

Close the top of the body

A white brick behind and a gray one in front of it. Neither is shaped: they are the course the shaped pieces sit on. Block the mass out square first, then clothe it — that way the bird is a bird at every stage.

Add these pieces
1 white 2 × 2 brick
1 light gray 2 × 3 brick
7

Cap the back with a ridged plate

A thin gray plate sloped on top on both sides, like the roof of a house — but asymmetrical, the left face longer than the right. One odd piece does more for the back than three ordinary ones would.

Add these pieces
1 light gray ridged plate
8

Raise the shoulder toward the neck

A gray plate levels the shoulder and a white slope eases it down toward the neck. Keep the run flat: the back is one long straight line from the tail, and a second rise here would break it into a row of spines.

Add these pieces
1 light gray 2 × 3 plate
1 white 2 × 2 slope
9

Cantilever a seat, then raise the neck

A brick reaching forward past the breast makes a landing for the neck, so the throat stands in front of the chest the way a crane's does. Then one long column, not a stack: the same long-piece-spans, short-piece-joins habit as the legs.

Add these pieces
1 light gray 1 × 2 brick (seat)
1 light gray 1 × 1 × 4 column
10

Set the head on the column

One brick — not two. A white round tile on its side is the eye, and it does more for the bird than any other single piece.

Add these pieces
1 black 2 × 2 brick
1 white 1 × 1 round tile
11

Add the beak, then pin it with a plate

The beak is a slope that stops short of a point, leaving a small upright wall at its tip. A thin plate then runs across the head and forward onto the beak, capping the head and trapping the beak at once — which is what holds a wedge that size on. A beak that did come to a point would have served just as well; none was in the bin. Printing one is a different matter.

Add these pieces
1 red 2 × 2 slope
1 black 2 × 3 plate
12

Finish with the golden crown

Three pieces, and they splay sideways rather than standing up in a tuft: an inverted slope flaring each way — top full and flat, underside swept away — with a cone between them. A wide golden fan is what names the bird from across a room.

Add these pieces
2 yellow inverted slopes
1 yellow cone
When it is standing. Set the finished bird beside the mosaic it came from and compare them: the neck too short, the body too narrow, the crown too tight. Every difference you can name is the next revision. Because the bricks come apart as easily as they go together, changing your mind costs nothing — which is exactly what makes a prototype worth building.
